newsitem.title: USA: CVS Corp-Revco makes sense - analysts.
newsitem.headline: CVS Corp-Revco makes sense - analysts.

text.p: A possible marriage between drug store chains CVS Corp, based in Rhode Island, and Ohio-based Revco D.S. Inc would make sense as it would put the resulting entity on more even footing with other giant drug chains in a consolidating industry.
The companies on Monday confirmed they were in merger talks but said there is no assurance a transaction will result.
If such a deal occurs, it could bring up to $45 a share for Revco shareholders including Chicago's Sam Zell and his Zell/Chilmark Fund LP which owns about 20 percent of Revco.
"It could be worth $44-$45" for Revco shareholders, said J.P. Morgan Securities analyst Mark Husson, who follows Revco.
"I would hope that CVS doesn't pay more than $45 a share," said Merrill Lynch's Gary Vineberg, who follows the drug store industry but does not follow CVS or Revco.
Revco shares spiked up a point in morning trading but by Monday afternoon were off 3/8 to 38-7/8 from Friday's close, CVS shares were off 5/8 to 42-1/2, both on the New York Exchange.
Revco last month acquired Alabama-based Big B Inc in a deal valued at $380 million. With its nearly 400 stores, Big B brought Revco to 2,600 stores in the Midwest and Southeast.
In the year ended in June, Revco earned $1.14 a share (including a $0.10 a share charge) on sales of $5.09 billion.
CVS has 1,408 stores in 15 states from Maine to Georgia and had revenues in the year just ended of $5.5 billion, a spokesman said.
CVS, the former Melville Corp, spun off a footwear business, discontinued some other businesses and in October changed its name to CVS, retaining the drug stores.
Drug chains are merging to fight drug pricing pressures in the era of managed care and health maintenance organizations.

Antitrust regulators' concerns about overlapping markets derailed a Rite Aid Corp friendly $1.8 billion bid for Revco last year. Rite Aid later acquired Thrifty Payless in a deal valued at $1.4 billion, giving Rite Aid more than 3,500 stores with annual revenues of more than $10 billion.

Another $10 billion-plus behemoth, Walgreen Co, has largely sat out consolidation, focusing instead on opening new stores for growth. The third giant is J.C. Penney Co's Thrift Drug Inc which is buying Eckerd Corp.
In the deal with Rite Aid Revco made it known it could be for sale, and with all the mergers in the industry, the list of available targets has dwindled, analysts said.
"Companies are not just buying earnings per share. They are buying leverage against the big third-party plan managers," J.P. Morgan's Husson said.
Merrill Lynch's Vineberg said smaller companies fear if they don't participate in the "merger and acquisition frenzy," they may become too small to compete effectively.
Vineberg said Revco could probably survive on its own, but is not as well positioned as the three giants or as well as CVS, which has higher sales per square foot.
In fact, he said, with a Revco deal, CVS may get many stores it does not want as the industry moves toward 10,000-sq.-ft.-plus freestanding stores.
McDonald & Co analyst Philip Muldoon said Revco could remain independent and viable even without a CVS deal.
"You don't necessarily have to be a $10 billion company to survive," Muldoon said. "It's a good business, and (Revco) just made an acquisition ...that's going to help them."
Eric Bosshard, an analyst with Midwest Research-Maxus Group, said CVS may face a challenge integrating a chain with little geographic overlap.
But overall, analysts said, the deal makes sense and is unlikely to face major regulatory hurdles since there is little geographic overlap.
